messages.author: 04cfbdc89f4c61fc
messages.subject: distsamp() modeling with many covariates
parts:
Dear unmarked developer,


I have collected 12 environmental covariates and wanted to get the best model to calculate the abundance. However, when I write the (~p, ~λ) part, it seems to have a huge number of possible combinations. 


I think the p and λ are independent, so I try to separate the project in two runs: one is (~p, ~1) and the other is (~1, ~λ). Each run generated 4,095 possible models. Then I take the least AIC model [(~pbest, ~1) and (~1, λbest)] from each run to combine as (~pbest, ~λbest). 


However, when I compare (~pbest, ~λbest) and (~1, λbest), it turns out the AIC of the latter one is smaller. I think this means potentially, there are other possible models that haven't been checked with this strategy exist. However, to run all possible combinations (4,095 x 4,095 = 16,769,025) seems not quite possible, as running 4,095 combinations took 3 days.


May I ask if there is way to efficiently get the best model?


Many thanks and best regards,


Yan

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: AW: [unmarked] Re: distsamp() modeling with many covariates
parts:
Dear Yan,

 

What capture-recapture and occupancy people usually do is a sequential approach to model selection: first optimize one part of the model using AIC, then keep the ‘optimal’ structure for that and proceed to optimizing the other part of the model. Typically, people start with the detection part, keeping the survival or occupancy part reasonably general (probably better than keeping it constant), and then keep the best structure for detection and optimize survival or occupancy (or abundance in your case).

 

That approach is of course not guaranteed to find the overall AIC-best model, but it seems to be a useful pragmatic approach that is widely used.

 

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.author: d9a48df2447ad4a0
messages.subject: Re: distsamp() modeling with many covariates
parts:
Dear Yan,

According to the papers I read, none of them have reach such a high number of covariates. Some papers stated that they tested all possible combinations of covariates but more papers didn't mention they did so. 

There is one recently published paper by Valenzuela-Sánchez et al. ("Assessing habitat quality when forest attributes have opposing effects on abundance and detectability: A case study on Darwin’s frogs"), mentioned an alternative of a two-stage ad hoc strategy. 

I tried the strategy but it seems there is very high chance that the best model is still hiding in the possible combinations untested by the strategy. 

My conclusion is that you have to try all the possible combinations to get the best model. Otherwise you may need an excuse for not testing all of them.

Best,

Q

messages.author: 05afbb8a30c1e331
messages.subject: Re: distsamp() modeling with many covariates
parts:
Yan,


I don't believe the p and λ portions of the hierarchical distance sampling model fit by unmarked::distsamp are independent.  You might look at a Bromaghin et al. 2013 paper (https://www.scirp.org/journal/PaperInformation.aspx?PaperID=27677) that provides an alternative model-selection process (called "Plausible Combinations") for cases like yours (i.e., cases where there are multiple submodels [p and λ] and you want to explore multiple covariates for each).  The authors compared this Plausible Combinations approach to the sequential approaches Marc mentioned, and an all-possible combinations approach.

Jason

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Re: distsamp() modeling with many covariates
parts:
Dear Qian,

I beg to differ: for better or worse, I don't think that you actually need to check out all possible combinations if you want to get your paper published. Over the past couple of years I must have seen dozens of papers who employed the sequential approach (and I am guilty of some of them myself). I am not saying that this is necessarily the best approach, but I just don't think that referees necessarily reject your paper if you do something other than the all-combinations approach, if this would involve fitting more than, say, 50-100 models.

And as a personal side comment: I think that model selection in the sense of a blind hunt for the lowest-AIC model is overrated anyway. I am not against trying to find one with an as low AIC as you can get, but don't spend sleep-less nights over the risk that you may have missed a model with even lower AIC. For two and a half reasons: first, there will always exist many, many models with lower AIC than the one you found (for instance, if you could get 'real good' explanatory variables, not the cheap proxies that you have). And second, because there are certainly cases where a model with dramatically low AIC can be totally useless, cf. in the case of many Nmix models with Negative binomial as opposed to a Poisson abundance mixture (see Kery, Ecology, 2018). And finally, there is much more to model selection than AIC-ology, see e.g. the monograph by Hooten & Hobbs (2015).

Side comment 2: I am not against model selection: I would do as good as I can, but at the same time remain somewhat relaxed about it.

Best regards  --- Marc
